name: Taloki
world_status: statement found in a copy already on file

earlier_scan.source_named: Mead, David E. 1999. The Bungku-Tolaki Languages of South-Eastern Sulawesi, Indonesia. Pacific Linguistics D-91.

new_statements.quote: In keeping with the focus on present-day languages, in this section I give an overview of current sound systems. All present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages are open syllable languages, with the only syllable patterns being V and CV. Most roots are disyllabic, though occasionally three and four syllable roots are found. Stress is penultimate (non-phonemic), with suffixation usually precipitating stress movement. [p.97:] I assume that in Proto-Bungku-Tolaki stress fell on the penultimate syllable, there being no reason to reconstruct otherwise. All present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages also exhibit penultimate stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable and is not contrastive; adding suffixes shifts stress rightward so it stays penultimate in the suffixed word. Stated for all present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages, a set that explicitly includes Taloki (TAL). Consistent Taloki-specific evidence: Mead 1999/1995 Taloki word lists carry no stress marks under a 'unmarked = penultimate' convention, and Mead 2020's phonetic forms are penult-stressed ([ˈʔihi], [moˈpiː], [ˈɗaːʔo]).
new_statements.exceptions: Mead 1998: none beyond stress shift under suffixation. Mead 2020 (Taaloki word list, p.9) notes the vocatives aˈmaː 'father!' and iˈndoː 'mother!' 'with stressed final syllable and lengthened vowel'; long vowels are analysed as VV sequences so forms like [moˈpiː] mopii are regular penultimate-vowel stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level generalisation in a comparative overview of present-day sound systems; supporting Taloki data are citation forms from elicited word lists (226-item survey list 1988; 844-item Sulawesi Long List, Mead 2020).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Mead 1998 p.16, p.97) is a family-wide generalisation over 'all present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages', a set Mead explicitly enumerates to include Taloki (TAL), p.11; it is not a Taloki-specific phonology. The only Taloki-specific description, Mead 2020 'Taaloki word list and notes' (community-preferred name Taaloki; = talo1252, Maligano village, respondent Drs. Lasamudi), gives no stress rule but its phonetic transcriptions show penultimate stress and it flags final stress only on two vocatives. Koroni (koro1311) and Kulisusu (kuli1254) are the closest relatives and were audited separately from the same sources.

sources.citation: Mead, David. 2020. Taaloki word list and notes. (Sulang Language Data and Working Papers: Word Lists, no. 11.) Sulawesi Language Alliance. 40 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 4 Sound system (pp.3-5): phonemes, syllable types V/CV/NCV, glottal stop, long vowels as VV; no explicit stress rule. Phonetic forms show penultimate stress (ihi [ˈʔihi], mopii [moˈpiː], ɗaaʔo [ˈɗaːʔo]); word-list items 108/110 vocatives aˈmaː 'father!', iˈndoː 'mother!' annotated 'with stressed final syllable and lengthened vowel' (p.9). p.2: nothing further of a linguistic nature written on Taaloki in two decades.

sources.note: Survey/overview. Taloki entry p.42: no phonology. Appendix 3 p.101 transcription convention (g): 'In the absence of any stress marking, one can assume penultimate stress occurring on the next to last written vowel.' The 76 TAL (Taloki) rows in the selected word lists (pp.103ff) carry no stress marks.
